title: Sudan’s children face a growing crisis of drone attacks and drought
subtitle: New UN findings document the expanding civilian toll of drone warfare, while failed rains threaten harvests and the services that keep children alive.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Drone strikes killed more than 1,630 civilians in Sudan between January and the end of October, the UN Human Rights Office said on 17 November, as attacks on essential infrastructure deepen a crisis for children already facing displacement, interrupted schooling and drought.

The figure is part of more than 2,230 civilian deaths the office confirmed over those ten months. It covers people of all ages, not children alone, and the UN cautions that the actual toll is likely higher. Its newly published report examines January to June; the accompanying announcement adds figures for the following four months. Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been fighting since April 2023.

For families, the danger extends beyond a strike itself. Electricity keeps water pumps running, health facilities operating and medicines cold. When those systems fail during a drought, children can lose access to clean water and treatment just as food becomes harder to obtain.
A shelter is no guarantee of safety

At Al Mina Al Bari, a displacement shelter in Al Obeid, North Kordofan, a drone strike late on 30 September reportedly killed one boy and injured 12 children, UNICEF said the following day. The injured included five boys and seven girls.

UNICEF’s Sudan representative, Angela Kearney, said families at the shelter had already fled their homes, some repeatedly. Her account describes a central problem for parents trying to protect children: reaching a displacement site does not necessarily mean reaching safety.

The damage also reaches children who survive without physical injury. UNICEF USA reported on 12 November that at least eight million children were out of school, mainly in Darfur and Kordofan. A September attack on a UNICEF warehouse in Al Obeid destroyed more than 292,000 textbooks and 40,000 Arabic-language and mathematics review books intended for children.

Care continues within families despite those losses. UNICEF USA described Hadia, a mother of seven in Al Obeid, who took in four surviving children of her sister after shelling killed their parents and some of their siblings. Such care preserves family ties, but it also leaves relatives responsible for more children’s food, health and schooling during a widening emergency.
The harvest cannot simply wait

Drought is damaging another source of protection: families’ ability to grow food. In its assessment dated 24 September, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization said rainfall shortages associated with El Niño had affected crop germination and establishment across Sudan’s growing areas.

In Sennar and Gedaref, which together normally produce about a quarter of Sudan’s sorghum, seasonal rainfall was about 20 and 30 per cent below the long-term average respectively. FAO’s satellite-based Agricultural Stress Index indicated severe drought conditions across substantial areas of cropland. These are indicators of crop stress, not a completed count of this season’s harvest losses.

Farmers also face insecurity, costly fuel and limited access to agricultural credit, FAO said. Its market monitoring showed sorghum prices more than doubled on average in most monitored markets between January and August. A poor harvest therefore meets households already struggling to buy their staple food.

Officials have disputed the likely scale of the loss. Reuters reported on 23 October that Agriculture Minister Esmat Qureshi had said the harvest would fall, but only modestly. Abdelrahman Ismail, head of the RSF’s humanitarian aid authority, told Reuters it had sought an early response and needed greater resources. Both sides deny accusations of obstructing aid.
Keeping children alive requires functioning services

UNICEF spokesperson James Elder warned on 10 November that electricity outages were stopping water pumps and treatment, threatening refrigerated medicines and making irrigation harder amid fuel shortages. He also reported pockets of cholera among communities that are difficult to reach, including displaced families.

UNICEF estimates that 825,000 children under five will suffer severe acute malnutrition during 2026. That is a projection of children needing treatment, not a death toll. The agency says it and its partners have treated hundreds of thousands of children, but its Sudan response was only one-third funded when Elder spoke.

Responsibility for the destruction remains central. The UN Human Rights Office attributed 29 strikes on electricity facilities and fuel stations across 11 states between 20 October and 4 November to the Rapid Support Forces. It said serious violations documented in its report may amount to war crimes. That is the office’s assessment, not a court judgment.

At the 17 November briefing, OHCHR’s Sudan representative Li Fung called for action against the continuing inflow of weapons, particularly drones, and for good-faith ceasefire negotiations. She also acknowledged a limitation in the data: drone deaths had not been systematically separated in the previous year’s records, preventing a straightforward year-on-year comparison.

For Sudan’s children, protection must be measured beyond the number of people who survive an attack. It also means a shelter that remains safe, a clinic able to treat illness, water that can be collected without danger and a classroom that can reopen. Repairing those services, allowing aid to reach families and preventing further attacks are inseparable parts of the response.
The Athena Perspective.
